sources.title: Roman Glass
sources.institution: Rosemarie Trentinella; The Metropolitan Museum of Art
sources.locator: 1 October 2003, Blown Glass section, web lines 150–153. English essay text on the /de/ route.
sources.originalChronology: Places glassblowing early in the first century BCE; this does not supply an exact invention year.
sources.scopedClaim: Identifies the Syro-Palestinian region as the origin and describes faster, more versatile manufacture.
sources.reuseTerms: Reference only; no source prose or images redistributed

sources.title: Glass of the Romans
sources.locator: Gallery description, web lines 91–93, especially the paragraph on hollow-tube inflation.
sources.asWorded: middle of the first century B.C.
sources.originalChronology: Places the innovation in the middle of the first century BCE, later than the Met essay's early-century wording.
sources.scopedClaim: Locates the innovation near Jerusalem and connects easier production with cheaper glass and wider availability.
sources.reuseTerms: Reference only; no source prose or images redistributed

sources.title: The Antikythera Shipwreck: The ship – the treasures – the Mechanism
sources.locator: Temporary exhibition page, 6 April 2012–29 June 2014; web lines 188–190. The exhibition dates are modern.
sources.originalChronology: Dates the sinking approximately 60–50 BCE. Its fourth- to first-century BCE range concerns the cargo objects, not the sinking.
sources.scopedClaim: A ship carrying luxury objects sank off Antikythera; its cargo illuminates Mediterranean trade.
sources.reuseTerms: Reference only; no source prose or images redistributed

sources.title: Stunning Finds from Ancient Greek Shipwreck
sources.locator: 9 October 2014, cargo description and excavation partnership at web lines 11–14; wreck date at line 20.
sources.originalChronology: Gives 70–60 BCE for the wreck. Its route and storm explanation are proposals, not established causes or destinations.
sources.scopedClaim: Describes art objects, luxury goods and the mechanism from the wreck investigated by WHOI and the Greek Ephorate of Underwater Antiquities.
sources.reuseTerms: Reference only; no source prose or images redistributed

sources.title: When was the ship wrecked?
sources.institution: Martin Allen; Antikythera Mechanism Research Project
sources.locator: FAQ main text, web lines 34–35. The same paragraph contains two differently bounded wreck estimates.
sources.originalChronology: The FAQ first gives 80–50 BCE from the contents, then concludes 85–60 BCE. Both are preserved; its 200 ± 43 BCE timber date is not a sinking date.
sources.scopedClaim: Supplies an additional, internally non-identical pair of wreck estimates based on the contents and coins. It does not justify a precise year.
sources.reuseTerms: Reference only; no source prose or images redistributed

sources.title: Les territoires gétules de Juba II
sources.institution: Jehan Desanges; Revue des Études Anciennes / Persée
sources.locator: 1964, volume 66, issues 1–2, pp. 33–47, DOI 10.3406/rea.1964.3713. Only the public HTML text of p. 33 was read: opening paragraph and footnote 2, web lines 38–44.
sources.originalChronology: The author explicitly fixes accession at 25 BCE using numismatic and literary arguments. This dataset performs no regnal-year conversion.
sources.scopedClaim: Juba II receives the Mauretanian kingdom through Augustus. The article questions parts of the ancient geographical tradition; exact frontier claims are excluded.
sources.reuseTerms: Reference only; no source prose or images redistributed

date.displayEn: First century BCE; early- and mid-century estimates
date.noteEn: The Met places the innovation early in the century; Corning places it near the middle. The numerical bounds cover their shared century, not a century-long invention process or evidence for the endpoint years.

events.summaryEn: Glassworkers in the eastern Mediterranean develop hollow-tube inflation of glass. The technique makes production faster and more adaptable, helping bring glass vessels to more people.
events.geographyEn: Syro-Palestinian region; Corning specifies the environs of Jerusalem
events.selectionNote: A major regional manufacturing innovation. Its differing museum chronologies remain explicit; neither an exact invention year nor the separate earlier invention of glass is asserted.

date.noteEn: The museum gives about 60–50 BCE and WHOI 70–60 BCE. The research-project FAQ gives both 80–50 and 85–60 BCE. The outer span accommodates these alternatives; the ship did not sink throughout it. Cargo and timber dates are separate.

events.titleEn: A merchant ship sinks off Antikythera
events.summaryEn: A ship carrying works of art, luxury goods and the Antikythera mechanism sinks off the island. Its varied cargo provides evidence of Mediterranean trade.
events.selectionNote: A notable trade assemblage, kept distinct from the manufacture of the mechanism and the modern discovery of the wreck. No precise sailing route, storm cause or exact sinking year is asserted.

date.noteEn: Desanges explicitly dates the accession to this year from numismatic and literary evidence. No month, day or exact territorial frontier is specified.

events.titleEn: Juba II becomes king of Mauretania
events.summaryEn: With Augustus's support, Juba II takes rule over the Mauretanian kingdom previously held by Bocchus.
events.selectionNote: A distinct political succession in North Africa, separate from Rome's military campaigns already catalogued. The entry retains the scholarship's stated year without converting regnal dates or adopting contested frontier descriptions.
